opus-5.5.text:
I like REPA a lot, and honestly it's less about the number in the paper and more about what it says about how I think vision research should go.

The idea itself is almost embarrassingly simple. You have a diffusion transformer, like DiT or SiT, learning to generate images by denoising. We asked: what are the hidden states inside this model actually learning? Are they learning good visual representations along the way? The answer was yes, somewhat, but not nearly as good as what a strong self-supervised model like DINOv2 has already learned. So we added one small regularization term. We take an intermediate layer of the diffusion model, project it, and align it with the clean-image features from a pretrained encoder. That's basically it. And training gets much faster, something like more than ten times faster to reach the same FID, and the final quality also improves.

Why do I like it so much? A few reasons.

First, for many years there's been this split in the community. On one side, people work on representation learning: self-supervised learning, contrastive learning, MAE, DINO, all of that. On the other side, people work on generative models. They're almost two different worlds, different conferences in spirit, different metrics, different intuitions. There's a long-standing belief, going back to Feynman's "what I cannot create, I do not understand," that generation should lead to understanding. REPA kind of flips that. It says maybe understanding can help generation, and that the bottleneck for a generative model is partly that it has to learn a good representation from scratch, which is very hard and very slow. If you give it a good representation to lean on, it doesn't need to struggle so much. To me that's a sign the two worlds should really be one.

Second, I just appreciate simple ideas that work. In research there's a temptation to build complicated systems with many components. REPA is a few lines of code. When something that simple gives you that much improvement, it usually means you've touched something real about the problem rather than engineering around it.

Third, and this matters to me personally, it validates the value of representation learning at a time when a lot of people were saying, "Self-supervised learning is done, everything is just scaling and language models now." REPA shows these visual representations are not just for linear probing benchmarks. They're useful building blocks, and they can make the most popular generative models today much better. That gives a kind of new life to the whole direction.

And finally, it opens up more questions than it answers, which I think is the mark of a paper I enjoy. Why does alignment help so much? Which layer should you align, which encoder? Should the generative model eventually learn representations as good as DINO on its own? Can you go the other way and have a single model that's great at both understanding and generation? Several follow-up works, ours and others, have started exploring this, and I think that's the most exciting part. It's less of an endpoint and more of a door.

r001.rationale: The response describes combining pretrained self-supervised visual representations with diffusion-model training, and frames this as a surprising bridge between two previously separate research communities.

fable-5.1.text:
Guest: I like REPA a lot, honestly, because of what it taught us rather than just the numbers. The result itself is simple to state: if you take a diffusion transformer and, during training, you align its intermediate features to a strong pretrained visual encoder like DINOv2, training gets dramatically faster, something like seventeen times fewer steps to reach the same FID on ImageNet. That is a big practical win. But the reason I care about it is the idea underneath.

For years there has been this divide in the field. On one side you have representation learning, self-supervised methods, contrastive learning, DINO, MAE, all of that. On the other side you have generative modeling, diffusion, flow matching. People mostly treated them as separate communities with separate goals. The generative folks cared about sample quality, the representation folks cared about linear probe accuracy, and nobody really asked whether one could help the other in a direct way.

What REPA shows is that a diffusion model is, internally, trying to learn a good representation of images, and it is actually pretty bad at it, or at least slow at it. If you probe the hidden states of a DiT or SiT during training, you see the representation quality slowly improving, and the generation quality tracks it. So the model is spending a huge amount of compute rediscovering semantic structure that a self-supervised encoder already knows. Once you just hand it that structure as a regularizer, the model can focus its capacity on the thing diffusion is actually good at, which is modeling the fine detail and the distribution. That is a clean, almost embarrassingly simple diagnosis of why these models are so expensive to train.

The other thing I appreciate is that it reframes the question of what the backbone is doing. It suggests the hard part of generation is not pixel synthesis, it is understanding. If understanding is the bottleneck, then all the progress in representation learning becomes directly relevant to generation, and vice versa. That opens up a lot of directions. Can generative training produce representations as good as DINO? Can we unify the two objectives in one model? Those were things people speculated about, and REPA gave us a concrete handle on them.

And finally, I just like papers where the method is a few lines of code and the insight is bigger than the method. You do not need a new architecture or a new loss landscape. You add one alignment term, and suddenly you learn something about the nature of the problem. Those are the papers that tend to shift how people think, and I think REPA did that.

r001.rationale: The response describes representation learning and generative modeling as previously separate areas, then presents REPA’s use of pretrained visual representations to guide diffusion training as a direct connection between them.

astra-6.text:
What I like about REPA is that it asks a very simple question: if we already have good visual representations, why should a generative model have to learn everything from scratch?

When you train a diffusion model, you ask it to predict noise or velocity, but along the way it also has to learn something about the structure of the image. That’s a lot to learn from one objective. REPA gives the model some guidance by aligning its intermediate features with representations from a pretrained vision encoder, like DINOv2.

And you’re still training a generative model. You’re just helping it develop useful representations more efficiently. A relatively simple auxiliary objective can make training faster and improve generation quality. That’s a very appealing result.

For me, the exciting part is the connection between representation learning and generation. We often treat them as separate problems, with separate methods and communities. REPA gives us a concrete example of how progress in one can help the other. I like papers where the method is simple, but the question it opens up is much bigger.

r001.rationale: The response connects representation learning with generation, but does not characterize REPA as an unexpected synthesis of prior work.

sol-6.1.text:
What I really like about REPA is that it asks a very simple question: if we already have good visual representations, why should a generative model have to learn everything from scratch?

A diffusion model is trained to predict noise or velocity, but to do that well, it also needs to understand the structure of the image. That understanding has to emerge indirectly through the generative objective. REPA gives it some guidance: align the model’s intermediate features with representations from a pretrained vision encoder, such as DINOv2. You keep the generative objective, but make the representation learning part easier.

And the nice thing is that this is just a training signal. You don’t need to run that additional encoder at inference time. So it’s a simple intervention that can improve both convergence and generation quality.

For me, the exciting part is the connection between representation learning and generation. We often treat them as separate problems, but REPA shows very concretely how progress in one can help the other. It also raises an interesting question: how much of the cost of training a generative model is actually spent learning a good representation?

r001.rationale: The response describes a connection between representation learning and generation, but does not characterize REPA as an unexpected synthesis of prior work.
